B, most likely — and there's a standard trick that shows it: shrink each average toward a prior by pretending every restaurant also has some phantom reviews. Suppose the typical restaurant rates 4.2 and we add 20 phantom reviews at 4.2 to each.

Restaurant A: (3 x 5.0 + 20 x 4.2)/23 = (15 + 84)/23 = 99/23, about 4.30.
Restaurant B: (900 x 4.6 + 20 x 4.2)/920 = (4,140 + 84)/920 = 4,224/920, about 4.59.

B wins after shrinkage. Three reviews can't establish perfection — one grumpy customer next week drops A to 4.0 — while 900 reviews pin B's quality down tightly. The phantom-review method (a simple Bayesian average) is roughly what rating platforms do behind the scenes, and the phantom count encodes how much evidence you demand before believing an extreme average.

General rule: distrust any average built on a handful of observations, especially a perfect or terrible one. Extremes on tiny samples are mostly noise wearing a crown.
Our school's pass rate jumped from 70% to 80% this year and the district is celebrating. The class has 10 students. Should they?

They should check the arithmetic of small numbers first: with 10 students, each student is worth exactly 10 percentage points. The jump from 70% to 80% is one student. One child having a good test day — or one family moving into the district — is the entire 'improvement.'

In a class of 100, one student is worth 1 point, and a 10-point jump means ten students changed outcomes: a signal worth investigating. Same headline percentage, completely different substance.

This is why year-to-year swings are wildest in small schools and why league tables of tiny units churn so dramatically. Before celebrating or panicking over a rate change, convert it back to counts: how many actual people moved? If the answer is one or two, you're reading noise as news.
I suspect my coin is biased because I flipped 7 heads out of 10. How strong is that evidence, exactly?

Weak. If the coin is perfectly fair, the chance of getting 7 or more heads in 10 flips is (C(10,7) + C(10,8) + C(10,9) + C(10,10))/1,024 = (120 + 45 + 10 + 1)/1,024 = 176/1,024, about 17.2%. A fair coin produces a result this lopsided — in one direction — about one time in six. (Counting both directions, 7-3 splits or worse happen about 34% of the time.)

For calibration: 8 or more heads has probability 56/1,024, about 5.5% — suggestive at best. Even 9 or more is 11/1,024, about 1.1%, which sounds damning until you remember how many coins get flipped in the world each day without anyone reporting the boring outcomes.

Ten flips simply can't resolve a coin. To detect a mild bias — say a coin that lands heads 55% of the time — you'd need on the order of a thousand flips before the signal climbs out of the noise.

A poll of 1,000 voters shows my candidate up 2 points, and the report brags about the youth vote: she's up 15 points among voters under 30. There were 80 voters under 30 in the sample. How much of this do I believe?

Believe the headline margin cautiously and the youth number barely at all. The full sample of 1,000 carries a margin of error of about ±3.1 points, so a 2-point lead is inside the noise — a statistical tie.

The youth subgroup is a different universe: with n = 80, the margin of error is 1.96 x sqrt(0.25/80), about ±11 points. A '15-point lead' among young voters is consistent with anything from a 4-point lead to a 26-point lead. Subgroups inherit the small sample, not the big poll's precision — the ±3 on the tin applies only to the whole sample.

This is one of the most reliable ways polls mislead without lying: the crosstabs get reported with the headline's confidence. Any subgroup claim should be read with its own n. When a campaign quotes a subgroup surge, ask how many actual respondents stand underneath it.
Our factory samples parts to estimate the defect rate. Sampling 100 parts gave us an estimate with about ±10 points of uncertainty. The boss wants ±5. 'So double the sample?' he asks. Answer him.

No — quadruple it. Uncertainty shrinks with the square root of the sample size, not in proportion to it. The margin of error behaves like 1/sqrt(n):

- n = 100: ±9.8 points (roughly your ±10)
- n = 400: ±4.9 points
- n = 1,600: ±2.45 points

Halving the error bars costs 4x the sampling; halving them again costs 16x the original. Precision is bought at a square-root exchange rate, which is why polls cluster around n = 1,000 (±3 points) — the next improvement is brutally expensive for a point or two of margin.

The boss's intuition fails because effort and precision feel like they should trade evenly. They don't. When someone proposes 'just sample a bit more' to settle a close estimate, check whether the needed precision is even affordable — often the honest answer is that the measurement can't resolve the question at any sane budget, and the decision has to be made another way.
What does it mean for betting odds to be 'fair,' and how do I spot when a bookmaker's odds aren't?

Odds are fair when the payout exactly balances the true probability, so the expected value is zero for both sides. Roll a die and bet on a 6: the true probability is 1/6, so fair odds pay 5:1 profit — you stake $1, and a win returns your stake plus $5. Check: (1/6) x 5 - (5/6) x 1 = 0.

Now suppose a bookmaker offers only 4:1 on the same bet. Your expected value per $1 staked becomes (1/6) x 4 - (5/6) x 1 = -1/6, about -$0.167 — a 16.7% house edge, far worse than most casino games.

The detection method generalizes: convert the offered payout into the probability it implies, and compare with your best estimate of the true probability. Offered 4:1 implies the bookmaker is pricing the event at 1/(4+1) = 20%, while the die says 16.7%. Whenever implied probabilities across all outcomes sum to more than 100%, the excess is the bookmaker's built-in margin — the vig — and it's the price of admission.
A single-number bet on roulette pays 35:1. Sounds generous. What's the house edge on American roulette (38 pockets) versus European (37)?

The payout pretends there are 36 pockets; the wheel disagrees. On an American wheel your number has probability 1/38. Expected value per $1: (1/38) x 35 - (37/38) x 1 = (35 - 37)/38 = -2/38, about -5.26%. The house keeps roughly 5.26 cents per dollar bet, on this and nearly every other bet on the layout.

On a European wheel with one zero: (1/37) x 35 - (36/37) = (35 - 36)/37 = -1/37, about -2.70%. Same game, same payout, half the edge — the entire difference is the American wheel's extra double-zero pocket.

This is the cleanest window into how casinos work: they don't cheat and don't need luck. They simply pay out as if the odds were slightly better for you than they are, and let volume and the law of large numbers collect the difference.
Why is 7 the most common total when you roll two dice? Give me the whole picture, including what it means for the craps come-out roll.

Because more dice combinations sum to 7 than to any other total. Enumerate all 36 equally likely outcomes and count by sum:

Totals 2 through 12 have counts 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1. So P(7) = 6/36 = 1/6, about 16.7%, while P(2) = P(12) = 1/36, about 2.8%. Seven wins by having the most parents: (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1).

In craps, the come-out roll wins immediately on 7 or 11: that's 6 + 2 = 8 outcomes, 8/36 = 2/9, about 22.2%. It loses immediately on 2, 3, or 12 ('craps'): 1 + 2 + 1 = 4 outcomes, 4/36 = 1/9, about 11.1%. Any other total becomes 'the point' and the roll continues.

The triangular distribution — rising to 7, falling after — is the signature of sums of independent dice, and the seed of the bell curve: add more dice and the totals cluster ever more tightly around the middle.
How does card counting in blackjack actually work? Movies make it look like memorizing every card and winning every hand.

The reality is bookkeeping plus patience, and the edge is small. The common Hi-Lo system assigns +1 to low cards (2-6), -1 to high cards (10s and aces), 0 to the rest. The running count tracks the balance of what has been dealt; divided by decks remaining, it estimates whether the shoe is rich in high cards, which favor the player (more blackjacks paying 3:2, more dealer busts when forced to hit stiff hands).

The size of the prize, stated as an approximation since it varies with rules and penetration: each point of true count is worth roughly half a percent of edge, so a strongly favorable shoe might give the counter about a 1% advantage — versus a disadvantage around 0.5% or worse in poor shoes, which is why counters bet big only when the count is high and sit out or bet minimum otherwise.

Even playing perfectly with a 1% edge, you still lose roughly half your hands; the profit is a slow statistical seep over thousands of hands, with wild swings along the way, and it requires a bankroll that can survive those swings. Casinos know all this, which is why they watch bet spreads rather than mind-read: counting isn't illegal, but they can simply refuse your action.

Poker decision: the pot is $100, my opponent bets $20, so it costs me $20 to call. I have a flush draw — 9 cards left in the deck will complete it, with 46 unseen cards and one card to come. Is calling profitable?

Yes, with a little room to spare. Pot odds first: after his bet the pot holds $120, and your $20 call makes $140 total. You break even if you win at least 20/140 of the time, about 14.3%.

Your draw: 9 winning cards among 46 unseen, 9/46, about 19.6%. Since 19.6% beats the 14.3% break-even, the call has positive expected value: on average you collect 0.196 x $140 = $27.40 for your $20, about +$7.40 per call over the long run.

Two honest caveats: this assumes you win every time you hit (he might hold a better hand even when your flush lands) and ignores future bets on the next street. Pot odds are the floor of poker math, not the whole building — but without them you're guessing, and with them this call is clearly right.
Three-card monte: you watch a queen among three face-down cards, bet, and pick. If it's a fair 1-in-3 guess and it pays 2:1, the game is fair, right? So why does everyone lose?

Your arithmetic about the fair version is correct — that's exactly what makes the con work. If the pick were genuinely random among three cards and the payout 2:1, expected value = (1/3) x 2 - (2/3) x 1 = 0. A fair game.

But the premise fails: the randomness isn't in the cards, it's in the operator's hands. Monte is sleight-of-hand — the operator controls where the queen actually is and can ensure the card you confidently tracked isn't the one you pick. Your probability of winning isn't 1/3; when real money is down, it's close to the operator's chosen rate, near zero, because the 'shuffle' is a performance. The free games and small bets you win early are marketing, dealt honestly to build your confidence.

The general lesson transfers far beyond street games: a probability calculation is only as good as the randomness it assumes. Before computing odds, ask who controls the randomizing mechanism and whether they profit from your loss. If the answer is 'the person offering the bet,' the stated odds are scenery.
In blackjack, the dealer shows an ace and offers 'insurance' — a side bet that the hole card is a ten, paying 2:1. Basic strategy charts say never take it. Prove it with numbers.

Count the unseen cards. Setting aside the dealer's ace and ignoring your own cards (the usual simplifying assumption): 51 cards remain unknown, of which 16 are ten-value (10s, jacks, queens, kings). So the probability the hole card is a ten is 16/51, about 31.4%.

Insurance pays 2:1, which would be fair at a probability of exactly 1/3, about 33.3%. Since 31.4% is less, the bet loses on average: expected value per $1 = 2 x (16/51) - 1 x (35/51) = (32 - 35)/51 = -3/51, about -5.9%.

So insurance is a side bet with a house edge near 6% — worse than the main game played well. The exception proves the rule: card counters take insurance when they know the remaining shoe is unusually rich in tens, pushing the true probability above 1/3. Without that knowledge, 'insuring' a good hand feels prudent and is simply a second, worse bet stacked on the first.
A $5 scratch card lists these odds: win $5 at 1 in 10, $10 at 1 in 25, $50 at 1 in 200, $500 at 1 in 5,000. What's the card actually worth?

About $1.25 — the game returns a quarter of its price. Multiply each prize by its probability:

- $5 x 1/10 = $0.50
- $10 x 1/25 = $0.40
- $50 x 1/200 = $0.25
- $500 x 1/5,000 = $0.10

Total expected value: 0.50 + 0.40 + 0.25 + 0.10 = $1.25 against the $5 price. The expected loss is $3.75 per card — a 75% house edge, dwarfing roulette's 5.26%.

Notice the design: most of the expected value sits in the small prizes, especially the $5 'win' that merely refunds your stake but feels like success and often gets reinvested on the spot. The $500 prize contributes a dime of value while doing all the advertising. Scratch cards are typically the worst-return gambling product sold legally — the printed odds table, which many jurisdictions require, convicts them if you take thirty seconds to do this multiplication.

Chuck-a-luck: bet $1 on a number from 1 to 6, roll three dice. You're paid 1:1 if your number appears once, 2:1 if twice, 3:1 if three times. It feels generous since you can win three ways. What's the actual edge?

The house keeps about 7.9% — the three ways to win are a curtain over the 125 ways to lose. Enumerate all 216 outcomes of three dice for your chosen number:

- Appears 0 times: (5/6)^3 of outcomes — exactly 125 of 216. You lose $1.
- Appears once: 75 of 216. You win $1.
- Appears twice: 15 of 216. You win $2.
- Appears three times: 1 of 216. You win $3.

Expected value: (75 x 1 + 15 x 2 + 1 x 3 - 125 x 1)/216 = (75 + 30 + 3 - 125)/216 = -17/216, about -$0.079 per $1 bet.

The seductive number is 'you win something 91 times out of 216,' about 42%. But most of those wins are the $1 consolation, and they don't offset the 58% of rolls where your stake vanishes entirely. Games that pay in several tiers are pricing each tier stingily — enumeration is the only antidote to the feeling of generosity.
Sports betting: both teams in a game are listed at -110 (bet $110 to win $100). If the teams are truly evenly matched, what does the bookmaker's pricing tell me?

It tells you the bookmaker takes about 4.8% off the top and that you must win 52.4% of such bets just to break even. Convert -110 to an implied probability: you risk 110 to profit 100, so the price implies a win probability of 110/(110 + 100) = 110/210, about 52.4%.

Both sides are priced at 52.4%, so the implied probabilities sum to about 104.8%. A real probability distribution must sum to 100% — the extra 4.8 points are the bookmaker's margin, the vig, built into every price.

Now the bettor's reality: if the teams are truly 50/50, each bet's expected value is 0.5 x 100 - 0.5 x 110 = -$5 on a $110 stake. To overcome the vig you need genuine forecasting skill worth at least 2.4 percentage points above the market's own estimate — against a counterparty who sets prices for a living. The vig is why 'I pick winners slightly more than half the time' still loses money.
A booth at the fair charges $1 to roll two dice and pays $5 if the total is exactly 7. My friend says the operator must be losing money since 7 is the most common total. Is he?

No — the game is exactly fair, which is almost as surprising. Seven is indeed the most likely total, with probability 6/36 = 1/6. The answer hinges on what 'pays $5' means. If the $5 is your total return (stake not refunded on top), the expected return is 5 x 1/6, about $0.83 on your $1, and the operator keeps about 17 cents per play. If instead you receive $5 profit plus your $1 back, the expected profit is 5 x (1/6) - 1 x (5/6) = 0 — perfectly balanced.

Under the profit reading, the fair payout for a 1-in-6 event is exactly 5:1, and the booth is offering it. The operator's business model there would be volume and the neighboring rigged games, not this one.

The general tool: an event with probability p has fair profit odds of (1-p)/p to 1. For p = 1/6, that's 5:1. Any payout shorter than fair odds is a toll; your friend's error was comparing the $5 prize to the $1 price without weighing the 5-in-6 chance of losing the dollar.
In keno, I pick 1 number out of 80 and the house draws 20 numbers. If my number is drawn I get paid $3 total on a $1 ticket (so $2 profit). It hits surprisingly often when I play. What's the catch?

The catch is that 'surprisingly often' is doing the selling, and the payout is priced for a much rarer event. Your number is among the 20 drawn with probability 20/80 = 25% — you'll 'win' one play in four, a very satisfying hit rate.

But the payout is only 2:1 profit. Expected value per $1: 0.25 x 2 - 0.75 x 1 = 0.50 - 0.75 = -$0.25. The house edge is 25% — five times roulette's, in the same league as scratch cards. Fair odds for a 25% event would pay 3:1 profit; you're offered 2:1.

Keno's design is the mirror image of the lottery: instead of a microscopic chance at a fortune, it offers a chunky chance at a payout that's secretly too small. Frequent small wins are the most effective camouflage a house edge can wear, because your memory counts wins, not net dollars.
Why are casinos so calm about variance? A player can win big on any given night, yet the casino's profit seems guaranteed. Put numbers on it.

Because the casino plays the game a million times while you play it fifty. Take $10 bets on red in European roulette: you win $10 with probability 18/37, lose $10 with probability 19/37. From the house's side, each bet earns on average 10/37, about $0.27, with a standard deviation of about $10 per bet.

Now scale to 1,000,000 bets. The house's expected profit is 1,000,000 x 0.27, about $270,000. The standard deviation of the total grows only with the square root of the number of bets: sqrt(1,000,000) x 10 = $10,000. So the house expects roughly $270,000, give or take about $20,000 (two standard deviations). A losing month is essentially impossible; the profit is a near-certainty wrapped around a predictable mean.

Meanwhile your 50 bets have an expected loss of about $13.50 with a standard deviation around $71 — your outcome is mostly luck, theirs is mostly law. The law of large numbers isn't a metaphor in this building; it's the business model. The casino sells variance to customers and keeps the average for itself.
